figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 1.   The IBIS is a collection of Transformer and Graphormer models designed to fully annotate bacterial metabolism. This suite classifies enzymes (e.g., via 
EC numbers), biosynthetic domains (e.g., Ketosynthase, Acyltransferase), and primary and specialized metabolic pathways. Furthermore, IBIS represents BGCs 
with meaningful embedded representations that reflect the chemical characteristics of encoded metabolites, thereby facilitating rapid, large-­scale comparisons 
across millions of BGCs. Inferences derived from bacterial genomes are integrated into the IBIS knowledge graph, which contextualizes these predictions by 
associating them with taxonomic and ecological niche information. Combining the IBIS suite with a comprehensive knowledge graph enables AI-­enhanced 
inference of the metabolic potential of bacteria.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 2.   Biosynthetic enzyme and domain identification with Transformers. (A) IBIS-­Enzyme maps each protein sequence to an embedded space, with proximity 
reflecting enzyme function similarity. It also predicts biosynthetic domain regions, which are further embedded by IBIS-­Domain to capture domain subtypes and 
substrate affinity. (B) The embedded space of protein sequences with EC classes not observed by IBIS-­Enzyme during training, projected into two-­dimensional 
space with UMAP. (C) Comparing IBIS-­Enzyme annotation coverage for SM against PFAM, antiSMASH, and PRISM. A two-­tailed t test is conducted to compare 
annotation distributions. ** means P-­value between 1e-­3 and 1e-­10 and *** means P-­value under 1e-­10. (D) Comparing IBIS-­Enzyme classification with ANN 
to predictions from CLEAN, DeepEC, and DeepECTransformer. In addition to EC number prediction, IBIS annotates curated protein families from SM (Protein 
Family), and identifies biosynthetic domains in protein megasynthases from nonribosomal peptide and polyketide biosynthesis (Biosyn. Domains). (E) Annotation 
speed of IBIS-­Enzyme ANN, DIAMOND, and hmmscan against the PFAM library.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 3.   Defining primary and SM with IBIS. (A; Left) ANN annotation of IBIS-­Enzyme embeddings labels proteins with KO labels and EC numbers. IBIS-­PM defines PM 
with curated rules based on KO and EC numbers. (A; Right) IBIS-­SM, a Graphormer model, defines SM from protein-­graph representations of successive genome 
slices, capturing protein functions with IBIS-­Enzyme embeddings and spatial organization between proximal ORFs through normalized nucleotide distances. 
IBIS-­SM predicts BGC membership and assigns plausible chemotypes to each ORF, aggregating predictions to define final BGC boundaries. (B) Comparing IBIS-­SM 
performance with the receiver-­operator characteristic curve (AUC) against existing rule-­based (PRISM, antiSMASH) and machine learning (DeepBGC, ClusterFinder) 
methods. We assess chemotype predictions on bacterial MiBIG BGCs and determine cluster boundaries using a manually curated dataset.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 4.   Large-­scale BGC embedding and comparison with IBIS-­BGC. (A) BGCs are visualized as interconnected data layers, comprising protein embeddings, 
domain embeddings, and chemotype assignments from IBIS-­Enzyme, IBIS-­Domain, and IBIS-­SM, respectively. IBIS-­BGC embeds this information into numerical 
representations, optimizing embedding distances to correlate with the chemical similarity of encoded metabolites. (B) Heat maps depicting correlation between 
Tanimoto molecular similarity and BGC distance similarity using IBIS-­BGC-­Embeddings and BIG-­SliCE pHMM feature vectors. Scores for Pearson’s linear correlation 
coefficient are shown above the plots. (C) A Two-­dimensional UMAP projection of the BGC landscape, representing BGC families from 121,056 bacterial genomes. 
IBIS identifies GCFs containing members associated with known BGCs (i.e., BGCs with established links to isolated metabolites). The production of the corresponding 
molecules was metabolically validated. The chemical structures illustrated in this figure represent examples of this validation. Novel derivatives of Xenoamicin 
and Aminocoumacin were successfully isolated and structurally characterized using NMR, further supporting the BGC–BGC relationships predicted by IBIS.
